---
title: "GPT and Transformers: architecture and data flow"
subtitle: "From tokens to next-token probabilities"
lang: en
---

::: {.chapter-lead}
A **GPT** is a language model based on an autoregressive Transformer: given a context of tokens, it estimates a distribution over the next token. To understand the system, distinguish the data flow, the learned parameters, and the generation loop. This page provides the overview; linked concept pages explain individual operations.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="The one-minute mental model"}
A GPT repeats the same loop: **represent the context → compute a distribution over the next token → select a token → append it to the context**. Attention lets positions exchange information; learned parameters determine the transformations being applied.

**First pass:** inspect the diagram, read sections 1–3, and remember this loop. You can leave the equations and interactive explorer for a second visit.

**Go deeper:** follow the attention calculation, try the interactive explorer, then use the linked concept pages. The mathematical details are optional depth, not an entry fee.
:::

## The full path, at a glance

![Simplified data flow of an autoregressive GPT, from tokens to next-token selection.](../images/gpt-data-flow-en.svg){fig-alt="Conceptual pipeline: text, tokenization, embeddings and position, repeated Transformer blocks, logits, softmax, next-token selection, then adding the token to the context." width=100%}

The diagram shows the conceptual path of generation. It intentionally omits implementation details such as residual connections, normalization, the key-value cache (KV cache), and sampling variants.

## 1. From text to representations

A tokenizer maps text to token IDs. An embedding matrix maps each ID to a learned vector. Positional information is also supplied, for example by adding a positional vector or by integrating position into attention as in [RoPE](positional-encoding.qmd).

An initial token embedding is not the same as a **contextual representation**: Transformer layers progressively update vectors using context. See [embedding space](embedding-space.qmd) for the representation basics, then explore [representation geometry and interpretability](embedding-space.qmd): [cosine similarity](cosine-similarity.qmd) and the [linearity hypothesis](embedding-linearity.qmd). [Tensors](tensors.qmd) explain how these representations are organised in computation.

## 2. Transformer blocks

A block combines two main operations:

- **Self-attention:** each position combines information from allowed positions. In GPT, a causal mask prevents access to future tokens.
- **Feed-forward network (MLP):** applies the same learned transformation independently to each position at this stage.

Blocks also include residual connections and normalization. Their exact order depends on the architecture: the diagram is an abstraction, not a specification of any particular model.

![Comparison of the roles of self-attention and the feed-forward network in a Transformer block.](../images/attention-vs-mlp-en.svg){fig-alt="Self-attention allows information to flow between allowed positions; the same feed-forward network is applied independently at each position." width=100%}

The important distinction is not that attention “understands” tokens while the MLP does not: both transformations are learned. Attention mixes information across positions; the MLP transforms each representation locally, with shared weights across positions.

### Follow the attention calculation

![Visual steps of attention: scores, optional mask, softmax and weighted sum of values.](../images/attention-calculation-flow-en.svg){fig-alt="Queries and keys produce scores. After scaling and optional masking, softmax creates weights that combine values into output vectors." width=100%}

1. [**Queries, keys, and values (Q, K, V)**](queries-keys-values.qmd) — three learned projections give representations distinct roles.
2. [**Scaled dot-product attention**](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd) — scores from $QK^\top$ are scaled by $\sqrt{d_k}$ and converted into weights by softmax.
3. [**Causal masking**](causal-masking.qmd) — excludes future positions before softmax.
4. [**Positional information**](positional-encoding.qmd) — supplies information about token order; the [positional encoding and RoPE lesson](positional-encoding.qmd) explains the mechanism in detail.

Attention weights are not a complete explanation of a prediction. They describe one aggregation step; projections, values, other heads, later layers, and the output projection also contribute.

## 3. From representations to probabilities

After the blocks, an output projection produces **logits**—unnormalized scores associated with the vocabulary. Softmax converts them into a probability distribution. A normalized distribution is not automatically calibrated or factually reliable: see [logits](logits.qmd), [probabilities](probabilities.qmd), and [likelihood](likelihood.qmd).

During generation, a selection rule chooses the next token: greedy selection, sampling, or a more elaborate method. The selected token is appended to the context, and the model runs again. Generation is therefore **autoregressive**; the model does not produce the whole response in a single prediction.

## Observe a Transformer in action

**[Transformer Explainer](https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/)**, developed at Georgia Tech, lets you explore a real GPT-2 small inference run in your browser. It complements this page's static diagrams: enter text and observe how representations, attention computations, and the next-token distribution evolve.

### A guided four-part exploration

1. **Tokens and representations.** Make a small change to the input text and inspect its tokenization. Connect tokens to IDs and embeddings in the [representation page](embedding-space.qmd).
2. **Attention.** Select tokens and inspect attention patterns. Relate scores, causal masking, and value aggregation to the pages on [Q/K/V](queries-keys-values.qmd), [attention](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd), and [causal masking](causal-masking.qmd).
3. **Prediction.** Inspect output scores (*logits*) and the vocabulary distribution. Use the pages on [logits](logits.qmd) and [probabilities](probabilities.qmd) to distinguish scores from probabilities.
4. **Decoding.** Change the temperature and, where offered by the interface, top-k/top-p settings. The same distribution can lead to different token selections; decoding does not change the model weights.

### Controlled experiments: move from observation to testing

To avoid drawing conclusions from a single visualization, keep a reference prompt, change **one factor at a time**, and record what changes.

1. **Tokenizer sensitivity.** Compare a word on its own, the same word preceded by a space, and a punctuation variant. Record tokens and IDs. Subword segmentation depends on the tokenizer and character context; it does not directly reveal the model's “understanding”.
2. **Causal masking.** Inspect the attention row for the final token, then append a suffix to the prompt. A position must not receive information from future positions. In a causal model in evaluation mode, prefix-position representations should remain invariant when a suffix is appended (up to numerical tolerance); this tests internal states, not just generated text.
3. **Temperature and sampling.** Keep the prompt and logits fixed, then change only temperature. The distribution changes according to \(p_i(T)=\operatorname{softmax}(z/T)_i\), while the raw logits remain identical. Then compare top-k and top-p: these filters change the set of allowed candidates. A sampled generation can vary even when prompt and settings are identical.

For each experiment, record the hypothesis, changed variable, observation, interpretation, and limitation. A visual observation is evidence to check against the equation and, where possible, an automated test.

The browser execution path uses Svelte/TypeScript, ONNX Runtime Web, and a GPT-2 tokenizer; `data.ts` calls the ONNX session. The repository also contains a PyTorch reference model in `model.py`, useful for inspecting the architecture and operations but distinct from the ONNX inference path used by the interface. This separation between computation, tensor extraction, visualization, and explanation is an architectural pattern to study, not one to copy wholesale into LLM Lab.

### Critical audit: a visualization is not a specification

The source code also exposes implementation choices to keep in mind:

- **Top-p:** `topPSampling` in `src/utils/data.ts` sorts the logits, keeps the top 50, applies temperature, then computes softmax and cumulative probabilities **over those 50 candidates only**. It truncates at threshold \(p\) and renormalizes the retained candidates. The restricted distribution therefore already sums to one, so the threshold is reached within this subset. The actual limitation is that tokens ranked below 50 are excluded before nucleus selection; if the exact nucleus over the full vocabulary would contain more than 50 tokens, this implementation cannot include them. For example, if the first 50 tokens carry only 60% of the full-vocabulary probability mass and \(p=0.9\), the tool renormalizes that 60% to 100%: the displayed threshold then corresponds to only 0.54 (= 0.9 × 0.60) of the original mass. Exact nucleus sampling over the full vocabulary must instead include tokens beyond rank 50 to reach 0.9. This is a tool-specific approximation, not a property of top-p itself.

**Conditional-distribution formulation.** Fix a temperature $T>0$ and let $P_T$ denote the softmax distribution that would be obtained over the full vocabulary after applying that temperature. Let $S_{50}$ be the retained set of 50 candidates and let $m=P_T(S_{50})<1$ be their mass under that distribution. After truncation, the implementation works with the conditional distribution $P_T(i\mid i\in S_{50})=P_T(i)/m$. For a retained prefix $A\subseteq S_{50}$, its cutoff condition becomes

$\sum_{i\in A}\frac{P_T(i)}{m}\geq p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_T(A)\geq p\,m.$

With $m=0.60$ and $p=0.90$, the prefix therefore needs only 0.54 of the original mass. Exact nucleus sampling over the full vocabulary instead accumulates $P_T$ until it reaches 0.90; because $S_{50}$ carries only 0.60, it must include tokens outside $S_{50}$.
- **Embeddings:** a learned vector representation is not a universal geometric definition of meaning. Similarity depends on the metric, space, layer, and task.
- **Attention:** displayed weights describe one computation step. They are not sufficient to measure a token's causal influence on the final logit.
- **Stochastic generation:** comparing two text outputs does not isolate a parameter's effect if the random draw also changes. To study the distribution, compare probabilities or control the random seed where the implementation allows it.

These observations do not invalidate the tool; they define precisely what it can teach and what should not be inferred from it.

### What this demonstration does — and does not — establish

- The tool runs **GPT-2 small (124 million parameters)**. It is a useful representative teaching model for core operations, not a substitute for inspecting every modern LLM architecture.
- Inference runs in the browser. The first load may download model assets and use your machine's memory and CPU.
- An attention-weight visualization shows one internal operation; by itself, it is not a causal or faithful explanation of the prediction.
- Generation settings such as temperature change next-token selection; they do not retrain the model or make its outputs factually reliable.
- This is an external demonstration. It does not execute LLM Lab's Python code and is not a test of our future implementations.

**Takeaway:** use the explorer to form hypotheses and locate operations; return to this site's equations to check them, then to repository tests and experiments when a corresponding implementation is available.

## Training and generation are not the same computation

During training, positions in an autoregressive sequence can be processed in parallel because the input-target shift and causal mask prevent future-token leakage. During ordinary generation, each next token depends on the context currently available, so the model advances step by step. Optimizations such as the KV cache avoid recomputing keys and values that have already been produced.

The objective—predicting the next token—remains the same, but the computation is organized differently.

## Limitations and common misconceptions

- **“A GPT is just an attention layer.”** No. It is an architecture with embeddings, repeated blocks, feed-forward transformations, residual connections, normalization, and an output head.
- **“Tokens are words.”** Not necessarily: a token can be a word, word fragment, punctuation mark, or another text fragment.
- **“A high probability guarantees a true answer.”** No. The distribution is learned to predict tokens in training data; factuality and calibration require separate evaluation.
- **“Attention weights reveal the model's reasoning by themselves.”** No. They do not establish the causal influence of a piece of information on the final output.
- **“All Transformers are GPTs.”** No. The original 2017 architecture used an encoder and a decoder; GPT is an autoregressive decoder-only family.

## Further reading, selected by purpose

You do not need to consume every resource. Choose one that answers your current question; return to the others when you want a different explanation or more technical depth.

### Build intuition with visuals

- [3Blue1Brown — *Transformers, the tech behind LLMs*](https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/gpt/): an animated system-level explanation of embeddings, Transformer blocks, logits, and generation.
- [3Blue1Brown — *Attention in transformers, step by step*](https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/attention/): a focused visual explanation of attention, masking, multiple heads, and cross-attention.
- [Jay Alammar — *The Illustrated Transformer*](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/): a step-by-step visual explanation of the **original encoder–decoder Transformer**. Use it to understand the 2017 design, not as a diagram of every modern GPT.
- [Jay Alammar — *The Illustrated GPT-2*](https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-gpt2/): a more directly relevant visual walkthrough of a decoder-only GPT-style model.

### Connect equations to an implementation

- [Vaswani et al. (2017), *Attention Is All You Need*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762): the primary paper for the original Transformer formulation. It describes an encoder–decoder architecture; GPT is a later decoder-only family.
- [Harvard NLP — *The Annotated Transformer*](https://nlp.seas.harvard.edu/annotated-transformer/): an annotated, executable implementation aligned with the original paper. It is valuable for connecting equations to code, but its architecture and training choices should not be treated as a specification for all modern LLMs.
- [PyTorch — Scaled dot-product attention](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html): the API contract for one operation, not a full explanation or implementation of a Transformer.

### Follow a structured learning path

- [Sebastian Raschka — *Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)*](https://www.sebastianraschka.com/llms-from-scratch/) and [the source repository](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch): a book-and-code path through data, attention, GPT implementation, pretraining, and fine-tuning. Use it as a substantial reference, not as the mandatory order of this site.
- [Raschka — reading recommendations](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch/blob/main/ch01/reading-recommendations.md): advice on first building a big-picture understanding, then reading alongside code.
- [DeepLearning.AI — *How Transformer LLMs Work*](https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/how-transformer-llms-work): a compact video course by Jay Alammar and Maarten Grootendorst, including tokenization, embeddings, attention, modern block components, and selected efficiency variants. Course access and terms may change.

These sources have different jobs: visual resources build intuition, the primary paper records the original formulation, annotated code exposes implementation choices, and API documentation specifies one library contract. They are complementary, not interchangeable. Where an explanation simplifies or an implementation makes a convention-specific choice, check the assumptions and scope before generalizing it.
